section: What are we going to build?
text:
What are we going to build?



Primary (essential) hypertension
Condition-based phenotype

Start with hypertension codelist
Create initial base cohort
Require ≥ 180 days prior observation

Restrict to adults (≥ 18 years)

Require a second hypertension record within 365 days
Exit at end of observation





Warfarin users
Drug-based phenotype

Start with warfarin codelist
Create initial exposure cohort
Require ≥ 365 days prior observation

Collapse exposures with a ≤ 30-day gap

Require 365-day washout

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
CodelistGenerator

The CodelistGenerator R package provides tools to


Explore OMOP CDM vocabularies available in the database
Generate codelists systematically using vocabulary-based search strategies
Generate codelist diagnostics to assess code use and identify potentially missing concepts

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Generating candidate concepts
Today, we’ll focus on the getCandidateCodes() function to identify candidate concepts for our two phenotypes.

getCandidateCodes(
  cdm,
  keywords,
  exclude = NULL,
  domains = "Condition",
  vocabularyId = NULL,
  standardConcept = "Standard",
  searchInSynonyms = FALSE,
  searchNonStandard = FALSE,
  includeDescendants = TRUE,
  includeAncestor = FALSE
)


The function returns candidate concepts for review, together with the search strategy used to identify them.
This allows us to define a systematic and reproducible codelist search strategy.

library(omock)

cdm <- mockCdmFromDataset(datasetName = "synpuf-1k_5.4", source = "duckdb")

Primary hypertension codelist







Note


A refined search strategy does not mean we have a final codelist.
CodelistGenerator helps us define a reproducible search strategy and generate a preliminary codelist.
Before cohort construction, this preliminary codelist is clinically reviewed.
Once cohorts are created, diagnostics provide further evidence to support additional codelist review and refinement.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Primary hypertension cohort

We will progressively apply our cohort inclusion criteria to identify adults with primary (essential) hypertension.

Create a base cohort from our essential hypertension codelist
Keep the first qualifying entry

Require ≥ 180 days of prior observation

Restrict to age ≥ 18 years

Require a second hypertension record within 365 days

Exit at end of observation

Warfarin cohort

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Warfarin cohort
→ Create treatment episodes and identify new users
We now combine nearby exposures into treatment episodes and apply our new-user criteria:

cdm$warfarin_new_users <- cdm$warfarin_base |>

  # Collapse exposures separated by ≤30 days
  collapseCohorts(
    gap = 30,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  ) |>

  # Require ≥365 days of prior observation
  requireDemographics(
    minPriorObservation = 365,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  ) |>

  # No warfarin exposure during the previous 365 days
  requireCohortIntersect(
    targetCohortTable = "warfarin_base",
    window = c(-365, -1),
    intersections = 0,
    name = "warfarin_new_users"
  )

PhenotypeR
PhenotypeR provides a standardised set of diagnostics to review and evaluate phenotypes created using the OMOP CDM.







Database diagnostics

databaseDiagnostics()








Codelist diagnostics

codelistDiagnostics()






Cohort diagnostics

cohortDiagnostics()








Population diagnostics

populationDiagnostics()

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Database Diagnostics
Summarise the database metadata including:

Snapshot
Summary of the person table

Summary of the observation period

Summary of the clinical tables (e.g., condition_occurrence) where concepts from the codelists defining the cohorts are found.









Note








Database diagnostics use functionality from OmopSketch.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Codelist Diagnostics

Summarise the codelist associated with your cohort including:


Achilles codes use (only if ACHILLES tables are present)

Orphan codes use (only if ACHILLES tables are present)
Cohort code use

Measurement code use (only if measurement concepts are present in your codelist)

Drug diagnostics (only if drug concepts are present in your codelist)










Note








Codelist diagnostics use functionality from CodelistGenerator to evaluate the use of concepts from our codelists in the OMOP CDM.
If the codelists contain measurement concepts, MeasurementDiagnostics is used to evaluate those concepts.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text: Cohort Diagnostics

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Cohort Diagnostics
Summarise and evaluate the cohorts including:

Cohort count & attrition

Cohort characteristics — Baseline characteristics of the cohort

Large-scale characteristics — Clinical records observed in different time windows

Compare cohorts — Overlap and timing between cohorts (if multiple cohorts)


Cohort survival — Survival until death (if death table is available)










Note








Cohort diagnostics use functionality from CohortCharacteristics to characterise and compare cohorts, and CohortSurvival to perform survival analyses.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Population Diagnostics

Contextualises the frequency of your study cohorts in the database calculating:

Incidence
Period Prevalence










Note








Population diagnostics use functionality from IncidencePrevalence to estimate the incidence and prevalence of our cohorts in the database population.

title: Creating cohorts from scratch using R
text:
Run diagnostics together
Rather than running each diagnostic separately, phenotypeDiagnostics() allows us to run them together.

result <- phenotypeDiagnostics(
  cohort,
  databaseDiagnostics = list(),
  codelistDiagnostics = list(),
  cohortDiagnostics = list(),
  populationDiagnostics = list()
)


We can choose which diagnostics to run and customise their parameters.

result <- phenotypeDiagnostics(
  cohort,
  databaseDiagnostics = list(),
  codelistDiagnostics = list(),
  cohortDiagnostics = list(
    cohortSample = 1000
  ),
  populationDiagnostics = NULL
)

section: Run diagnostics of hypertension and warfarin cohorts together
text:
Run diagnostics of hypertension and warfarin cohorts together
We created our two cohort separately. To run phenotyper, we can bring them together into a single cohort table and then run PhenotypeR functions to this table.

cdm <- bind(
  cdm$essential_hypertension,
  cdm$warfarin_new_users,
  name = "phenotypes"
)
cdm$phenotypes |> settings()

Run phenotype diagnostics

Now we can evaluate both phenotypes using the same standardised diagnostic workflow.

Then we can use the function shinyDiagnostics to create a shinyApp to review results:



shinyDiagnostics(result = result, directory = here())

title: Using LLMs with PhenotypeR
text:
Caveats
I will be showing you what you can do, not what you should do


Creating LLM tools for phenotyping is relatively easy. Creating tools that are trusted, improve the quality of research, and provide a good user experience is the hard part.



Choice of model undoubtedly matters. But not clear which model is best, by how much, or for which task.



System prompts and user input can also have a dramatic impact on the results.



Closed-weight cloud-based models show performance drift, making validation even harder.

title: Using LLMs with PhenotypeR
text:
More caveats
Reliance on LLM tooling in OHDSI can increase barrier to entry, especially if tools are tied to specific providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc)


And even more so if tools need access to other paid-for APIs (e.g. clinical resources)

title: Using LLMs with PhenotypeR
text:
Even more caveats
Low quality health research is prevalent


Reproducibility crisis in health research



LLM integration can go both ways. Increasing risk of OMOP-slop vs additional context and double-checking.

title: Using LLMs with PhenotypeR
text:
ellmer
We’ll be using the ellmer R package for interacting with LLMs.


Provides a simple interface for working with LLMs in a consistent manner.



Building on ellmer, we can add model-agnostic support with users choosing the model to use.

title: Using LLMs with PhenotypeR
text:
Unstructured chat
We can work with a simple, unstructured, chat.

chat_medgemma$chat("Summarise the clinical presentation of hypertension")

Hypertension clinical presentation encompasses elevated blood pressure 
readings, commonly assessed via ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) or 
office blood pressure measurements. Symptoms range from asymptomatic to those 
associated with target organ damage (e.g., headache, dizziness, visual 
disturbances, chest pain, shortness of breath, peripheral edema). Key clinical 
features also include hypertension-related conditions like stroke, heart 
failure, kidney disease, and cardiovascular disease.  Patient risk factors 
influencing hypertension include age, genetics, ethnicity, obesity, physical 
inactivity, sodium intake, excessive alcohol consumption, and stress.

title: Using LLMs with PhenotypeR
text:
Unstructured chat

chat_medgemma$chat("What are the demographics of people presenting with hypertension")

Hypertension prevalence varies by age, with increasing incidence from middle 
age onward. Higher rates are observed in African Americans, Hispanics, and 
individuals with a family history of hypertension or those residing in specific
geographic regions. Socioeconomic factors, including access to healthcare and 
healthy food options, also contribute to disparities.

title: Using LLMs with PhenotypeR
text:
Unstructured chat
Bad idea:

chat_medgemma$chat("What clinical codes should I use to identify hypertension in my  OMOP CDM?")

For OMOP CDM, consider using ICD-10 codes such as I10 (Essential (Primary) 
Hypertension), I11 (Secondary Hypertension), I15 (Hypertensive Heart Disease), 
I17 (Renovascular Hypertension), I25 (Hypertensive Kidney Disease), I22 
(Hypertensive Cardiovascular Disease), I40-I45 (Specific Hypertension), and 
potentially others depending on the specific manifestation of the condition.  
Consider using UMLS concepts or SNOMED CT for more granularity.

section: Designed first for open-weight locally-hosted models
text:
Designed first for open-weight locally-hosted models

Available to all of the OHDSI community




Smoother package development (easy to implement, cheaper, and straightforward to test)





Easy to switch to using frontier models (and see if they are worth the extra cost).





But 6+ months behind “state-of-the-art”. (Although allows us to learn from experience of others)

title: Using LLMs with PhenotypeR
text:
Human-in-the-loop

Designed to support the human phenotyper, not automate them away.




All LLM-generated artefacts can be inspected, reviewed, and edited.





Main use of LLM is to provide additional context making it easier to double-check results

title: Using LLMs with PhenotypeR
text:
Benchmarking LLM performance
We can use the vitals package to test how closely LLM output matches known clinical benchmarks.

library(vitals)
vitals::vitals_log_dir_set(tempdir())

age_benchmark <- tibble(
  input = "Summarise the clinical presentation and typical age at diagnosis of hypertension",
  target = "50"
)

score_within_5_years <- function(samples) {
  est_age <- purrr::map_int(samples$solver_metadata, "average_age_at_diagnosis")
  target_age <- as.integer(samples$target)
  
  list(
    score = factor(
      ifelse(abs(est_age - target_age) <= 5, "Pass", "Fail"),
      levels = c("Fail", "Pass"), 
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )
}

chat_medgemma_fresh <- chat_medgemma$clone()
chat_medgemma_fresh$set_turns(list())
chat_medgemma_fresh$set_system_prompt(system_prompt)

age_task <- Task$new(
  dataset = age_benchmark,
  solver = generate_structured(
    solver_chat = chat_medgemma_fresh,
    type = type_object(
      clinical_summary = type_string(
        description = "Brief 1-sentence summary of the presentation."
      ),
      average_age_at_diagnosis = type_integer("Estimated average age in years")
    )
  ),
  scorer = score_within_5_years
)

age_task$eval(epochs = 10, view = FALSE)

text:
Tool calling
We can incorporate tool calling. But note we can’t use them directly with structured chat. We first have to use chat for the tool to be run, and then extract out into structured chat.

library(ellmer)
library(httr2)
chat <- chat_google_gemini(model = "gemini-4-argon")

search_hecate_standard_concepts <- function(query) {
  req <- request("https://hecate.pantheon-hds.com/api/search_standard") |>
    req_url_query(q = query)
  resp <- req_perform(req)
  resp_body_string(resp)
}

hecate_tool <- tool(
  search_hecate_standard_concepts,
  name = "search_hecate",
  description = "Search the OHDSI Hecate semantic search engine for standard concepts",
  arguments = list(
    query = type_string(
      "The medical term or condition related to my search.",
      required = TRUE
    )
  )
)

chat$register_tool(hecate_tool)

chat$chat(
  "Use the Hecate tool to search for 'hypertension' and list all returned concepts."
)

section: Grounding expectations with a trusted source
text:
Grounding expectations with a trusted source
We can download a clinical guideline (e.g., NICE NG136: Hypertension in adults) and extract its text so models are grounded in authoritative up-to-date guidance

library(pdftools)

Using poppler version 25.09.1

nice_url <- paste0(
  "https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/resources/",
  "hypertension-in-adults-diagnosis-and-management-pdf-66141722710213"
)
nice_pages <- pdf_text(nice_url)
nice_context <- paste(nice_pages[5:12], collapse = "\n")

chat_nice <- chat$clone()$set_turns(list())$set_system_prompt(paste(
    system_prompt,
    "\n\nBase your answers on this NICE NG136 guideline excerpt:\n",
    nice_context
  ))

chat$chat(
  "Summarise approach to diagnosing for hypertension according to NICE."
)

According to the **National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) 
guideline NG136** (*Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management*), the 
diagnosis of hypertension is a stepped process that relies on confirming 
elevated clinic readings with out-of-office measurements.

Here is a summary of the NICE approach to diagnosing hypertension:

---

### 1. Initial Clinic Blood Pressure Measurement
* **Preparation:** Ensure the patient is seated, relaxed, and in a quiet 
environment. Palpate the radial or brachial pulse before measuring (if the 
pulse is irregular, measure blood pressure manually, as automated devices may 
be inaccurate).
* **Both Arms:** At the first assessment, measure blood pressure in both arms. 
If the difference in readings between arms is more than **15 mmHg**, repeat the
measurements. If the difference remains more than 15 mmHg on the second 
measurement, use the arm with the **higher** reading for all subsequent 
measurements.
* **Multiple Readings:** If the first clinic blood pressure reading is **140/90
mmHg or higher**, take a second measurement during the consultation. If the 
second measurement is substantially different from the first, take a third 
measurement.
* **Recording:** Record the **lower** of the last two measurements as the 
clinic blood pressure.

---

### 2. Confirming the Diagnosis (ABPM or HBPM)
Do not diagnose hypertension based on a single clinic visit unless it is a 
hypertensive emergency. 

* **If Clinic BP is between 140/90 mmHg and 180/120 mmHg:**
  * **Gold Standard – ABPM (Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring):** Offer ABPM
to confirm the diagnosis. Ensure at least 2 measurements per hour are taken 
during the person’s usual waking hours (e.g., 08:00 to 22:00). Use the average 
value of at least **14 measurements** taken during waking hours to confirm the 
diagnosis.
  * **Alternative – HBPM (Home Blood Pressure Monitoring):** If the person is 
unable to tolerate ABPM, offer HBPM. The patient should take two consecutive 
measurements (at least 1 minute apart) while seated, twice daily (ideally 
morning and evening) for at least **4 days** (ideally 7 days). Discard the 
measurements taken on the first day and use the average value of all the 
remaining measurements to confirm the diagnosis.

* **If Clinic BP is 180/120 mmHg or higher (Severe Hypertension):**
  * **Refer for same-day specialist review** if there are signs of:
    * Retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema (accelerated/malignant hypertension).
    * Life-threatening symptoms (e.g., new-onset confusion, chest pain, signs 
of heart failure, or acute kidney injury).
    * Suspected phaeochromocytoma (e.g., labile or postural hypotension, 
headache, palpitations, pallor, diaphoresis).
  * **If no same-day referral is indicated:** Carry out investigations for 
target organ damage as soon as possible:
    * If target organ damage is identified, consider starting antihypertensive 
drug treatment immediately without waiting for ABPM/HBPM results.
    * If no target organ damage is identified, confirm diagnosis using 
ABPM/HBPM (or repeat clinic BP within 7 days).

---

### 3. Diagnostic Thresholds (Staging)

Hypertension is diagnosed and staged using **both** clinic and ABPM/HBPM 
averages:

| Stage | Clinic Blood Pressure | **AND** ABPM / HBPM Average |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Stage 1 Hypertension** | 140/90 mmHg to 159/99 mmHg | **135/85 mmHg to 
149/94 mmHg** |
| **Stage 2 Hypertension** | 160/100 mmHg to 179/119 mmHg | **150/95 mmHg or 
higher** |
| **Stage 3 (Severe) Hypertension** | **Systolic ≥ 180 mmHg** OR **Diastolic ≥ 
120 mmHg** | *(Confirmed via clinical assessment/ABPM as above)* |

*(Note: If Clinic BP is ≥ 140/90 mmHg, but the ABPM/HBPM average is < 135/85 
mmHg, this is considered **White-Coat Hypertension**).*

---

### 4. Concurrent Assessments (While Waiting for Confirmation)
While awaiting ABPM or HBPM confirmation, NICE recommends completing two vital 
assessments for all patients with suspected hypertension:

1. **Cardiovascular Risk Assessment:** Use a formal risk assessment tool (such 
as **QRISK3**) to estimate the patient's 10-year risk of cardiovascular 
disease.
2. **Investigations for Target Organ Damage:**
   * **Urine:** Test for haematuria using a reagent strip, and send a urine 
sample to test for the albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) to check for proteinuria.
   * **Bloods:** Measure electrolytes, creatinine, estimated glomerular 
filtration rate (eGFR), total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, and HbA1c.
   * **Eyes:** Examine the fundi for the presence of hypertensive retinopathy.
   * **Heart:** Arrange a 12-lead electrocardiograph (ECG) to check for left 
ventricular hypertrophy or other cardiac abnormalities.

title: Using LLMs with PhenotypeR
text:
Grounding with ragnar & embed_google_gemini()

Instead of pasting all the NICE guideline into the prompt, ragnar chunks the document and uses embed_google_gemini() to index each chunk as a semantic vector in DuckDB:

library(ragnar)
library(pdftools)
chunks <- pdf_text(nice_url) |> 
  paste(collapse = "\n") |> 
  MarkdownDocument(origin = nice_url) |> 
  markdown_chunk()
store <- ragnar_store_create(
  location = ":memory:",
  embed = embed_google_gemini()
)
ragnar_store_insert(store, chunks)
ragnar_store_build_index(store)


chat_nice_rag <- chat$clone()$set_turns(list())$set_system_prompt("You are an expert clinical phenotyper. Answer strictly using retrieved NICE NG136 excerpts.")
ragnar_register_tool_retrieve(
  chat = chat_nice_rag,
  store = store,
  store_description = "NICE NG136 hypertension guideline chunks"
)
chat_nice_rag$chat(
  "According to NICE NG136, what blood pressure thresholds define Stage 1 vs Stage 2 hypertension?"
)

that define Stage 1 and Stage 2 hypertension?", ...)

  #> "origin":
"https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng136/resources/hypertension-in-adults-diagnosis-and-management-pdf-66141722710213",


  #> "doc_id": 1,

According to the **NICE NG136** guideline (*Terms used in this guideline*), the
blood pressure thresholds that define Stage 1 and Stage 2 hypertension are:

### **Stage 1 Hypertension**
* **Clinic blood pressure:** Ranging from **140/90 mmHg to 159/99 mmHg**
* **AND subsequent ABPM daytime average or HBPM average:** Ranging from 
**135/85 mmHg to 149/94 mmHg**

---

### **Stage 2 Hypertension**
* **Clinic blood pressure:** **160/100 mmHg or higher**, but **less than 
180/120 mmHg**
* **AND subsequent ABPM daytime average or HBPM average:** **150/95 mmHg or 
higher**

*(Note: A clinic systolic blood pressure of 180 mmHg or higher or a clinic 
diastolic blood pressure of 120 mmHg or higher defines **Stage 3 or severe 
hypertension**.)*
